## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. Use the positive-energy joint spectral input: a
nonzero complex Hilbert space
$\mathcal H$, a strongly continuous translation representation
$U:\mathbb R^4\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, a projection-valued measure $E$ on
$\mathbb R^4$ with $U(a)=\int e^{ip\cdot a}\,dE(p)$ and
$E(\mathbb R^4\setminus\overline V_+)=0$, and an invariant unit cyclic vacuum
$\Omega$ for a specified unital $*$-subalgebra $\mathfrak A\subseteq
\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, meaning
$\overline{\{B\Omega:B\in\mathfrak A\}}=\mathcal H$. The pairing is
$p\cdot a=p^0a^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf a$.
Use the shell coordinates and signature of the scalar future mass shell
definition: for $m>0$ and $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$,
$\omega_m(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+m^2}$ and
$p_m(\mathbf k)=(\omega_m(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)$. Here $m$ is the positive
inverse-length mathematical shell parameter called $\mu$ in that supplier;
it is not identified with a measured rest mass. The coordinates have length
units, $\mathbf k$ and $\omega_m$ have inverse-length units, and
$\mathbf k/\omega_m(\mathbf k)$ is dimensionless.

$\mathcal M_m=\{(p^0,\mathbf p):(p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=m^2,\ p^0>0\}$
is the positive mass shell; it is closed and hence Borel. Its equivalent
parameterization is $\mathcal M_m=\{p_m(\mathbf k):\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3\}$.
It is an isolated massive shell input when $P_m:=E(\mathcal M_m)\ne0$ and some
$0<\delta<m$ satisfies
$$E\bigl(\{p\in\overline V_+:|\sqrt{(p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2}-m|<\delta\}\setminus\mathcal M_m\bigr)=0.$$
The corresponding one-particle space in this contract is the closed subspace
$\mathcal H_m=P_m\mathcal H$. This is an adopted spectral hypothesis and
subspace designation; the definition does not infer particle stability from a
formal two-point-function pole.

A translation-covariant local net is an assignment
$O\mapsto\mathfrak A(O)$ of unital $*$-subalgebras of
$\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ to bounded open $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, with
$\mathfrak A(O)\subseteq\mathfrak A$, such that $O_1\subseteq O_2$ implies
$\mathfrak A(O_1)\subseteq\mathfrak A(O_2)$,
$U(a)\mathfrak A(O)U(a)^*=\mathfrak A(O+a)$, and
$A_1A_2=A_2A_1$ for every $A_i\in\mathfrak A(O_i)$ when the regions are
spacelike separated. Spacelike separation means
$(x^0-y^0)^2-|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|^2<0$ for every
$x\in O_1,y\in O_2$. An operator $A$ is local if it belongs to
$\mathfrak A(O)$ for some bounded open $O$. A bounded operator $A$ is
norm-almost-local if, for every integer $N\ge1$, there is a constant
$C_N<\infty$ and operators $A_R\in\mathfrak A(O_R)$ for all $R\ge1$, where
$O_R=\{x:|x^0|+|\mathbf x|<R\}$, such that
$\|A-A_R\|\le C_N(1+R)^{-N}$. The domain version of almost locality uses a
common dense translation-invariant domain $\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ with
$\Omega\in\mathscr D$: $A$ and each local approximant $A_R$ act on
$\mathscr D$, and for every $\xi\in\mathscr D$ and integer $N\ge1$ there is
$C_{N,\xi}<\infty$ such that
$\|(A-A_R)\xi\|\le C_{N,\xi}(1+R)^{-N}$ for all $R\ge1$. A local or
almost-local operator is an interpolator for $f$ if $A\Omega$ is defined and
the vector below is nonzero.

For fermionic fields, the corresponding operator net is a $\mathbb Z_2$-graded
field net: each local algebra splits as
$\mathfrak F(O)=\mathfrak F_0(O)\oplus\mathfrak F_1(O)\subseteq\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$
and has a grading
automorphism $\gamma$ with $\gamma(A)=(-1)^aA$ for homogeneous
$A\in\mathfrak F_a(O)$, $a\in\{0,1\}$. Graded locality means
$AB=(-1)^{ab}BA$ for homogeneous $A\in\mathfrak F_a(O_1)$ and
$B\in\mathfrak F_b(O_2)$ in spacelike separated regions. The graded net has
the same isotony and translation covariance conditions. The local or
almost-local interpolators used in that branch, their grading, and the
statistics assignment are construction inputs.

$\ell_0>0$ denotes the fixed length represented by one numerical unit of the
time parameter. A smooth compact momentum packet is a smooth compactly supported function
$f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$; its support is the closure of
$\{\mathbf k:f(\mathbf k)\ne0\}$. Extend it to the bounded Borel function
$\widehat f(p^0,\mathbf p)=f(\mathbf p)$ on $\mathbb R^4$ and write
$\Phi_E(\widehat f)=\int\widehat f\,dE$ for its bounded PVM integral.
For a bounded interpolating operator $A$, define the one-particle packet
vector
$$\psi(A,f)=\Phi_E(\widehat f)P_mA\Omega\in\mathcal H_m.$$
The integral is a bounded operator by the bounded Borel PVM integral theorem;
it commutes with $P_m$ because both are functions of the same PVM. Its shell
support lies in the compact Borel set
$S_{m,f}=\{p_m(\mathbf k):\mathbf k\in\operatorname{supp}f\}$, so the
equivalent projection form is $E(S_{m,f})\Phi_E(\widehat f)A\Omega$.
The velocity support is
$V_m(f)=\{\mathbf k/\omega_m(\mathbf k):\mathbf k\in\operatorname{supp}f\}$.
Packets have disjoint velocity supports when these sets are pairwise
disjoint.

The associated scalar positive-energy packet solution, with fixed Fourier
normalization, is
$$u_{m,f}^\eta(t,\mathbf x)=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(\mathbf k)e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-i\eta\ell_0t\omega_m(\mathbf k)}\,d^3\mathbf k.$$
For each fixed $t$, this is smooth in $\mathbf x$ and rapidly decreasing
together with all spatial derivatives, meaning that for every
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$ and integer $N\ge0$,
where $\partial_{\mathbf x}^\alpha:=\prod_{j=1}^3
\partial_{x_j}^{\alpha_j}$,
$\sup_{\mathbf x}(1+|\mathbf x|)^N|\partial_{\mathbf x}^{\alpha}
u_{m,f}^\eta(t,\mathbf x)|<\infty$. Indeed, the momentum integrand and all
its derivatives are smooth and compactly supported, so repeated integration
by parts in $\mathbf k$ gives these bounds. Let
$\alpha_a(A)=U(a)AU(a)^*$ for $a\in\mathbb R^4$. For bounded local or
almost-local $A$, define the candidate smeared operator by the strong operator
integral
$$A_t^\eta(f)=\mathrm{s}\!\!\int_{\mathbb R^3}u_{m,f}^\eta(t,\mathbf x)\,\alpha_{(\eta\ell_0t,\mathbf x)}(A)\,d^3\mathbf x.$$
The rapid-decay estimate with $N=4$ is integrable on $\mathbb R^3$, since in
spherical coordinates $\int_0^\infty r^2(1+r)^{-4}\,dr<\infty$. Strong
continuity of $U$ and boundedness of $A$ therefore make the vector-valued
integral well defined on each vector, and
$\|A_t^\eta(f)\|\le\|A\|\|u_{m,f}^\eta(t,\cdot)\|_{L^1}$. With the stated
translation and Fourier conventions, its mass-shell component on $\Omega$ is
exactly $\psi(A,f)$. Indeed,
$\alpha_{(\eta\ell_0t,\mathbf x)}(A)\Omega
=U(\eta\ell_0t,\mathbf x)A\Omega$
has spectral multiplier $e^{i\eta\ell_0tp^0-i\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x}$;
Fourier inversion in the convention of the supplier listed under Definition
references, after the rescaling $\mathbf k=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$, gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}u_{m,f}^\eta(t,\mathbf x)e^{-i\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x}\,d^3\mathbf x=f(\mathbf p)e^{-i\eta\ell_0t\omega_m(\mathbf p)}.$$
On $\mathcal M_m$ the remaining time multiplier is
$e^{i\eta\ell_0t(p^0-\omega_m(\mathbf p))}=1$, yielding
$P_mA_t^\eta(f)\Omega=\Phi_E(\widehat f)P_mA\Omega$. Convergence of the full vector
$A_t^\eta(f)\Omega$ to that component is a separate construction obligation.
For a domain-valued variant, the corresponding integrals and all products
must instead be defined on the common invariant domain. Use the completed Hilbert tensor powers and their unitary
permutation action: $S_n$ is the permutation group of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and
$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)
=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)}$ on elementary tensors.
The sign $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)$ is $+1$ for an even permutation and $-1$
for an odd permutation. The orthogonal symmetrizing and antisymmetrizing
projections are $P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$. For
$\sigma\in\{s,a\}$, the Fock space
$\mathcal F_\sigma(\mathcal H_m)$ is the square-summable direct sum of the
ranges of these projections for $n\ge1$, together with vacuum sector
$\mathbb C$ at $n=0$; use the componentwise second-variable-linear inner
product and vacuum
conventions of the previously defined QFT Fock spaces, with
$P_{\sigma,n}=P_{s,n}$ for $\sigma=s$ and $P_{\sigma,n}=P_{a,n}$ for
$\sigma=a$. The finite packet
domain $\mathcal D_\sigma$ is the linear span of the vacuum and the
$P_{\sigma,n}$-projections of elementary tensors built from
$\psi(A_j,f_j)$ with pairwise disjoint velocity supports. The selected value
of $\sigma$ and, for fermionic fields, any required graded locality are
construction inputs.

For such a finite packet family $(A_j,f_j)_{j=1}^n$, a candidate
Haag–Ruelle approximant is
$\Psi_t^\eta=A_{1,t}^\eta(f_1)\cdots A_{n,t}^\eta(f_n)\Omega$, where
$t\ge1$ is the dimensionless positive-time parameter, physical coordinate
time is $\eta\ell_0t$, and $\eta\in\{+1,-1\}$ labels outgoing ($+1$) or
incoming ($-1$) scattering. The operators
$A_{j,t}^\eta(f_j)$ act on a common dense domain $\mathscr D$ invariant under
translations and these operators, with $\Omega\in\mathscr D$; every displayed
product is required to be defined there. Bounded operator families are the
special case $\mathscr D=\mathcal H$.
The operator families are supplied by the chosen construction. The one-particle limit condition is
$A_{j,t}^\eta(f_j)\Omega\to\psi(A_j,f_j)$ in norm as $t\to\infty$.
On the zero-particle vacuum label $1\in\mathbb C$, set
$\Psi_t^\eta(1)=\Omega$ for every $t$.
For each $f\in\mathcal D_\sigma$, the construction supplies a linear map
$\Psi_t^\eta:\mathcal D_\sigma\to\mathcal H$ whose values on elementary
packet tensors are these operator products; the assignment must be
well-defined independently of a tensor presentation. The Cook condition is
that $t\mapsto\Psi_t^\eta(f)$ is norm-$C^1$ on
$[1,\infty)$ and, for constants $C_{\eta,f}\ge0$ and
$\epsilon_{\eta,f}>0$,
$$\left\|\frac{d}{dt}\Psi_t^\eta(f)\right\|\le C_{\eta,f}(1+t)^{-1-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}\qquad(t\ge1).$$
Norm-$C^1$ means that the norm derivative exists for each $t>1$, has the
corresponding one-sided derivative at $t=1$, and is norm-continuous on
$[1,\infty)$.
The parameter $t$ is the dimensionless numerical time in the fixed coordinate
unit; changing that unit changes $C_{\eta,f}$ but not integrability. A construction
must also establish any required convergence of approximant inner products to
the specified $\mathcal F_\sigma(\mathcal H_m)$ inner products. The joint
spectral input states cyclicity but not uniqueness of the invariant vacuum;
any vacuum uniqueness or clustering hypothesis needed for this convergence
must be stated or proved separately.

This is a contract for a proof, not an existence theorem. It does not derive
the Cook bound, the one-particle limits, or the Fock inner-product limits from
locality and shell isolation. An actual construction must also record uniform
bounds on the vector approximants; those bounds are distinct from bounds on
the operator factors $A_{j,t}^\eta(f_j)$.
thm-qftx-cook-scattering-limit:
## Statement

Let $\mathcal D_\sigma$ and the direction-labelled packet families
$\Psi_t^\eta(f)\in\mathcal H$ be as in the massive scattering approximant
contract, with
$\eta\in\{+1,-1\}$, $f\in\mathcal D_\sigma$, and $t\ge1$. Assume that for
each fixed $\eta,f$, the map $t\mapsto\Psi_t^\eta(f)$ is continuously
differentiable in Hilbert-space norm and
$$\left\|\frac{d}{dt}\Psi_t^\eta(f)\right\|\le C_{\eta,f}(1+t)^{-1-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}$$
for constants $C_{\eta,f}\ge0$ and $\epsilon_{\eta,f}>0$. Then the norm limit
$W_\eta f=\lim_{t\to\infty}\Psi_t^\eta(f)$ exists and
$$\|\Psi_t^\eta(f)-W_\eta f\|\le \frac{C_{\eta,f}}{\epsilon_{\eta,f}}(1+t)^{-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}.$$
In particular, each approximant family is uniformly bounded in norm. Write
$(f,g)_{\mathcal F,1}:=\langle g,f\rangle_{\mathcal F,2}$ for the
first-variable-linear pairing corresponding to the QFT Fock definition's
second-variable-linear pairing. If $f\mapsto\Psi_t^\eta(f)$ is linear on
$\mathcal D_\sigma$ and its pairwise first-variable inner products converge
to $(f,g)_{\mathcal F,1}$, then $W_\eta$ is an isometry on
$\mathcal D_\sigma$ and extends uniquely to an isometry on its Hilbert-space
closure. The derivative estimate alone does not assert this inner-product
convergence or that the range is all of $\mathcal H$.
prop-qftx-scattering-isometry-not-comple:
## Statement

Let $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}=\overline{\mathcal D_\sigma}$ and let
$\Omega_\pm:=W_{\pm1}:\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}\to\mathcal H$ be the two
isometric extensions supplied by the preceding Cook theorem after its
pairwise Fock-inner-product
hypothesis is proved. Define the comparison operator
$S=\Omega_+^*\Omega_-$. Here the Hilbert adjoint $T^*$ of a bounded map
$T:H_1\to H_2$ is characterized by
$(Tx,y)_{H_2}=(x,T^*y)_{H_1}$, a contraction satisfies
$\|Sx\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$, an isometry is a linear inner-product-preserving
map, and unitary means a surjective isometry. Then
$S$ is a contraction. It is unitary if and only if
$\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+=\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_-$. Full asymptotic
completeness is the stronger condition
$\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+=\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_-=\mathcal H$; this
stronger condition is not part of the unitary-on-common-range criterion.

## Statement

def-csm-frontier-local-topologies:
## Definition

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a finite nonempty alphabet $S$ with the discrete topology, and a bijective enumeration $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ of $\mathbb Z^d$. For a finite set $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and assignment $a\in S^F$, the cylinder set determined by $(F,a)$ is $[F,a]=\{\sigma\in\Omega:\sigma|_F=a\}$. The cylinder sigma-algebra $\mathcal C$ is generated by these sets.

For each finite $F$, let $\pi_F:\Omega\to S^F$ be restriction to $F$. For probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal C)$, local weak convergence $\mu_n\to_{\mathrm{loc}}\mu$ means that $(\pi_F)_*\mu_n(B)\to(\pi_F)_*\mu(B)$ for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and every $B\subseteq S^F$. Equivalently, all finite-coordinate cylinder probabilities converge. The cylinder sigma-algebra is shown below in a local result to equal the Borel sigma-algebra, with local weak convergence equal to ordinary weak convergence on this space.
def-csm-frontier-vague-topology:
## Definition

Fix $d\ge1$. A locally finite counting measure on $\mathbb R^d$ is a measure of the form $\xi=\sum_{r\in I}\delta_{x_r}$, where $I$ is finite or countable, repetitions among the points $x_r\in\mathbb R^d$ are allowed, and every compact set contains only finitely many listed points, counting repetitions. The empty sum is allowed and is the zero measure. For a Borel set $B$, $\xi(B)$ is the number of listed points in $B$, with multiplicity. Write $\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$ for the set of these measures. For $x\in\mathbb R^d$, the point mass $\delta_x$ assigns mass $1$ to a Borel set containing $x$ and mass $0$ otherwise.

The vague topology on $\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$ is the coarsest topology for which $\xi\mapsto\int f\,d\xi$ is continuous for every nonnegative continuous compactly supported function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$. Thus $\xi_n\to_{\mathrm v}\xi$ exactly when $\int f\,d\xi_n\to\int f\,d\xi$ for every such $f$.

Here a random locally finite counting measure means a measurable random element for which $\Xi_n(B)$ is a random variable for every bounded Borel set $B$. If $(\Xi_n)$ is a sequence of such measures on a common probability space and $K$ is compact, its local counts are uniformly integrable on $K$ when

$$\lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_n\mathbb E\!\left[\Xi_n(K)\mathbf1_{\{\Xi_n(K)>R\}}\right]=0.$$

This is the count-tail condition used when an argument needs control of unbounded observables supported in $K$. The definition asserts no convergence of expectations without the exact test-function, support, and tail hypotheses of the result being applied.
def-csm-frontier-finite-generator-chain:
## Definition

Let $E=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for a finite integer $m\ge1$. A rate matrix on $E$ is a real matrix $L=(L_{ij})_{i,j\in E}$ such that $L_{ij}\ge0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\sum_{j\in E}L_{ij}=0$ for every $i$. Write $\lambda_i=\sum_{j\ne i}L_{ij}$, so $L_{ii}=-\lambda_i$. The row convention acts on a column observable $f:E\to\mathbb R$ by $(Lf)(i)=\sum_jL_{ij}f(j)$; a row probability vector evolves by right multiplication.

Fix an initial probability vector $\nu$ on $E$ and put $q=\max_i\lambda_i$. If $q=0$, then $L=0$ and the associated realization is the constant process $X_t=Y_0$ with $Y_0\sim\nu$. If $q>0$, put $R=I+L/q$, a stochastic matrix. A uniformized realization consists of a probability space carrying a discrete-time Markov sequence $(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ with initial law $\nu$ and transition matrix $R$, and independent random variables $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ that are independent of the entire sequence $Y$ and satisfy $\mathbb P(W_n>u)=e^{-qu}$ for $u\ge0$. Here a discrete-time Markov sequence with transition matrix $R$ means that
$$\mathbb P(A\cap\{Y_{n+1}=j\})=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A R_{Y_nj}]$$
for every $n\ge0$, $j\in E$, and $A\in\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)$. Each $W_n$ therefore has the exponential distribution of rate $q$; in particular its mean is $q^{-1}$. On its null complement set $N_t=0$ and $X_t=Y_0$. The construction filtration is $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(N_s,X_s:0\le s\le t)$; it records event counts and states through time $t$ and is not completed or made right-continuous by this definition.

This uniformized construction permits reducible rate matrices and states with zero exit rate. A local existence result proves that every finite rate matrix and initial law admit such a realization and that its conditional transition matrices are $e^{tL}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^nL^n/n!$.

## Statement

## Statement

$$D(p\|q)=\sum_{z:p(z)>0}p(z)\ln\frac{p(z)}{q(z)},$$

$$D(P\|Q)=D(P_X\|Q_X)+\sum_{x:P_X(x)>0}P_X(x)D(P_{Y|x}\|Q_{Y|x}).$$

$$D(P\|Q)\ge d(P(C)\|Q(C)),\qquad d(a\|b)=a\ln\frac ab+(1-a)\ln\frac{1-a}{1-b},$$

## Statement

## Statement

## Statement

## Statement

def-qsmx-von-neumann-algebra:
## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.
def-qsmx-conjugate-hilbert-space-and-ant:
## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. All inner products are linear in their first
argument. If $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, its **conjugate Hilbert space**
$\overline H$ consists of symbols $\overline x$ for $x\in H$, with
$\overline x+\overline y=\overline{x+y}$,
$a\,\overline x=\overline{\overline a\,x}$ for $a\in\mathbb C$, and
$$\langle\overline x,\overline y\rangle_{\overline H} :=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle_H}.$$
The canonical map $c_H:H\to\overline H$, $c_Hx=\overline x$, is a
conjugate-linear surjective isometry.

For complex Hilbert spaces $H_1,H_2$, a linear operator $A$ is a linear map
$A:D(A)\to H_2$ on a linear domain $D(A)\subseteq H_1$. Its graph is
$\Gamma(A)=\{(x,Ax):x\in D(A)\}\subseteq H_1\oplus H_2$, with the direct-sum
Hilbert norm. It is densely defined when $D(A)$ is dense in $H_1$, and closed
when $\Gamma(A)$ is closed.

For a densely defined linear operator $A:D(A)\subseteq H_1\to H_2$, define
$D(A^*)$ to consist of those $y\in H_2$ for which
$x\mapsto\langle Ax,y\rangle_{H_2}$ is bounded on $D(A)$ in the $H_1$ norm.
The bounded functional extends uniquely to $H_1$; its Riesz vector
$A^*y\in H_1$ is specified by
$$\langle Ax,y\rangle_{H_2}=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_{H_1} \qquad(x\in D(A)).$$
This defines the linear adjoint $A^*:D(A^*)\subseteq H_2\to H_1$.

An operator $S:D(S)\subseteq H\to H$ is **antilinear** when
$S(ax+by)=\overline a\,Sx+\overline b\,Sy$. Its associated linear operator
$\widetilde S:D(\widetilde S)\subseteq\overline H\to H$ is
$D(\widetilde S)=c_H(D(S))$ and
$\widetilde S(\overline x)=Sx$. For densely defined antilinear $S$, define
$$S^*:=c_H^{-1}\widetilde S^*,$$
on the domain $D(S^*)=D(\widetilde S^*)$. Thus $S^*$ is antilinear and
$$\langle Sx,y\rangle_H=\langle S^*y,x\rangle_H \qquad(x\in D(S),\ y\in D(S^*)).$$
lem-qsmx-trace-class-duality:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, and let
$\mathcal S_1(H)$ be its trace-class operators with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
and trace $\operatorname{Tr}$. Finite-rank operators are dense in
$(\mathcal S_1(H),\|\cdot\|_1)$. For every bounded linear functional
$\Phi:\mathcal S_1(H)\to\mathbb C$, there is a unique $X\in\mathcal B(H)$ such

## Statement

lem-qsmx-monotone-bounded-positive-net:
## Statement

nonempty directed set, and let $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ be a net in $M$ such that each

## Statement

## Statement

def-qsmx-von-neumann-algebra:
## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.
def-qsmx-conjugate-hilbert-space-and-ant:
## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. All inner products are linear in their first
argument. If $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, its **conjugate Hilbert space**
$\overline H$ consists of symbols $\overline x$ for $x\in H$, with
$\overline x+\overline y=\overline{x+y}$,
$a\,\overline x=\overline{\overline a\,x}$ for $a\in\mathbb C$, and
$$\langle\overline x,\overline y\rangle_{\overline H} :=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle_H}.$$
The canonical map $c_H:H\to\overline H$, $c_Hx=\overline x$, is a
conjugate-linear surjective isometry.

For complex Hilbert spaces $H_1,H_2$, a linear operator $A$ is a linear map
$A:D(A)\to H_2$ on a linear domain $D(A)\subseteq H_1$. Its graph is
$\Gamma(A)=\{(x,Ax):x\in D(A)\}\subseteq H_1\oplus H_2$, with the direct-sum
Hilbert norm. It is densely defined when $D(A)$ is dense in $H_1$, and closed
when $\Gamma(A)$ is closed.

For a densely defined linear operator $A:D(A)\subseteq H_1\to H_2$, define
$D(A^*)$ to consist of those $y\in H_2$ for which
$x\mapsto\langle Ax,y\rangle_{H_2}$ is bounded on $D(A)$ in the $H_1$ norm.
The bounded functional extends uniquely to $H_1$; its Riesz vector
$A^*y\in H_1$ is specified by
$$\langle Ax,y\rangle_{H_2}=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_{H_1} \qquad(x\in D(A)).$$
This defines the linear adjoint $A^*:D(A^*)\subseteq H_2\to H_1$.

An operator $S:D(S)\subseteq H\to H$ is **antilinear** when
$S(ax+by)=\overline a\,Sx+\overline b\,Sy$. Its associated linear operator
$\widetilde S:D(\widetilde S)\subseteq\overline H\to H$ is
$D(\widetilde S)=c_H(D(S))$ and
$\widetilde S(\overline x)=Sx$. For densely defined antilinear $S$, define
$$S^*:=c_H^{-1}\widetilde S^*,$$
on the domain $D(S^*)=D(\widetilde S^*)$. Thus $S^*$ is antilinear and
$$\langle Sx,y\rangle_H=\langle S^*y,x\rangle_H \qquad(x\in D(S),\ y\in D(S^*)).$$
lem-qsmx-trace-class-duality:
## Statement

## Statement
